1. Meeting the Patient & Vital Signs

Meeting Your Patient

Listening to the heart has come to epitomize the art of bedside diagnosis. Mastering cardiac examination requires patience, practice, and repetition — a skill increasingly at risk from evolving technology and the time constraints of modern practice.

  • Introduce yourself; confirm the patient's name and date of birth
  • Explain the purpose of the exam; obtain consent
  • Adjust the bed to a 45° angle; wash your hands
  • Begin by inspecting the patient from the end of the bed
  • Evaluate the patient from the waist up (offer a gown/blanket to maintain modesty)
  • Expose the patient's legs to look for venous changes, edema, ulceration, etc.
  • Ask about pain or discomfort throughout the exam
Section 1.1

Q1. Before beginning a cardiovascular exam, a student adjusts the bed and prepares to inspect the patient. Which of the following best reflects the recommended initial approach?

The recommended approach starts with introductions, consent, and hand hygiene, followed by inspecting the patient from the end of the bed — including exposing the legs, since venous changes, edema, or ulceration there are relevant cardiovascular findings.

Vital Signs & Postural Blood Pressure

Objective measurements come first: temperature, blood pressure, pulse (regular/irregular; brady/tachycardic), and respiratory rate with O2 saturation.

  • Blood pressure in both arms: a significant difference between arms raises concern for aortic dissection.
  • Blood pressure sitting and standing: a significant drop identifies postural (orthostatic) hypotension.
Section 1.2

Q2. A patient's blood pressure is found to be substantially different between the right and left arms. Which condition should this finding raise concern for?

A significant difference in blood pressure measured between the two arms is a classic finding suggesting aortic dissection, which is why blood pressure should ideally be checked in both arms.
Section 1.2

Q3. A patient's blood pressure drops significantly when moving from sitting to standing, accompanied by lightheadedness. What is this finding called?

A significant drop in blood pressure when changing from sitting to standing defines postural (orthostatic) hypotension — which is why BP should be checked in both positions.

Section 1 Summary Table

ConceptKey Point
Meeting the patientIntroduce, confirm ID, explain/consent, 45° bed angle, hand hygiene, inspect from end of bed, expose waist-up and legs, ask about pain throughout
Vital signs checkedTemperature, blood pressure, pulse (rate/rhythm), respiratory rate/O2 sat
BP in both armsA significant difference suggests aortic dissection
BP sitting & standingA significant drop identifies postural (orthostatic) hypotension

2. General Inspection

Inspection Findings

Many clues to cardiac pathology come from simple visual inspection, before ever touching the patient or stethoscope.

  • Increased work of breathing: can reflect several cardiac pathologies, ranging from pericarditis to congestive heart failure.
  • Cyanosis: suggests low tissue oxygen saturation and needs prompt attention. Cardiac causes are usually congenital (right-to-left shunting) or due to abnormal/low hemoglobin.
  • Pallor: suggests anemia or reduced perfusion — though it may simply be the patient's natural complexion.
  • Bedside paraphernalia: note oxygen, ECG leads, indwelling catheters (monitoring urine output), and the number of pillows used (patients with heart failure often prop themselves up with extra pillows to breathe more easily).
  • Peripheral edema: often visible in the lower limbs without needing a focused JVP exam.
  • Jugular venous distension (JVD): reflects right-sided heart pressure; may be visible just from positioning.
  • Cachexia: suggests advanced heart failure.
  • Scars: a midline sternotomy scar may indicate a prior CABG ("cabbage"), valve replacement, or congenital correction — check the entire knee, leg, and ankle too, for saphenous vein harvesting scars.
Section 2.1

Q4. A patient with known type 2 diabetes has a midline sternotomy scar and additional linear scars along the medial aspect of the leg and ankle. What does this combination of scars most likely indicate?

A midline sternotomy scar can result from a prior CABG, valve replacement, or congenital correction. When accompanied by scars along the leg/ankle, this suggests saphenous vein harvesting for a CABG — so the entire leg should be checked for these scars whenever a sternotomy scar is found.
Section 2.1

Q5. A patient with cardiac cyanosis is found to have a right-to-left cardiac shunt. Which category of heart disease does this most likely reflect?

Cardiac causes of cyanosis are usually congenital in nature, due to a right-to-left cardiac shunt (or due to abnormal hemoglobin) — distinguishing it from most acquired adult cardiac conditions.

Facial Inspection

Eye contact with the patient offers its own diagnostic clues:

Facial Signs and Cardiac Associations
Facial SignDescriptionPossible Cardiac Association
Malar flushRedness around the cheeksMitral stenosis
XanthomataYellowish lipid deposits around the eyes, palms, or tendonsHyperlipidemia
Corneal arcusA ring around the corneaAge, hyperlipidemia
ProptosisForward projection/displacement of the eyeball; occurs in Graves' diseaseAtrial fibrillation
Section 2.2

Q6. A patient has a persistent, symmetric redness across both cheeks. Which valvular condition is classically associated with this facial finding?

A malar flush (redness around the cheeks) is classically associated with mitral stenosis.
Section 2.2

Q7. A patient with Graves' disease is noted to have proptosis on exam. Which cardiac arrhythmia is this facial finding associated with?

Proptosis occurs in Graves' disease, and hyperthyroidism (as in Graves' disease) is a well-known precipitant of atrial fibrillation.

3. Hands, Pulses & Peripheral Vascular Exam

Pulse Rate, Rhythm & the Collapsing Pulse

Taking the pulse is one of the simplest, oldest, and most informative clinical tests. Palpate the right radial pulse to assess rate and rhythm; character and volume are easier to detect in larger arteries (brachial, carotid).

  • Irregular rhythm: commonly atrial fibrillation or ectopic beats; also bundle branch blocks or re-entrant tachycardias.
  • Radio-radial delay (comparing left and right radial pulses): a sign of aortic coarctation or aortic dissection.
  • Radio-femoral delay: also seen in coarctation/dissection.

Collapsing Pulse Test

With your left hand, hold the patient's right elbow and feel for the brachial pulse; with your right hand, feel the radial pulse. Keep your hands in position and briskly (but gently) lift the patient's arm above the level of the heart, holding it there.

Abnormal finding: a collapsing ("water-hammer") pulse — a gushing retraction of blood during diastole — is a classic sign of aortic regurgitation.
Altered Pulse Characteristics
Type of PulsePulse CharacteristicsMost Likely Cause
Regularly irregular—2nd-degree heart block, ventricular bigeminy
Irregularly irregular—Atrial fibrillation, frequent ventricular ectopics
Slow risingLow gradient upstrokeAortic stenosis
Waterhammer, collapsingSteep up and down stroke (lift arm above heart height)Aortic regurgitation, patent ductus arteriosus
BisferiensA double-peaked pulse — second peak may be smaller, larger, or equal to the firstAortic regurgitation, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Pulsus paradoxusExaggerated fall in pulse volume on inspiration (>10 mmHg on sphygmomanometry)Cardiac tamponade, acute asthma
BoundingLarge volumeAnemia, hepatic failure, type 2 respiratory failure (high CO₂)
Pulsus alternansAlternating large and small volume pulsesBigeminy
Section 3.1

Q8. While examining a patient with a known murmur, a physician holds the patient's arm above heart level and notes a gushing, "water-hammer" retraction of blood during diastole. This collapsing pulse is a classic sign of which condition?

A collapsing (water-hammer) pulse — a gushing retraction of blood felt during diastole when the arm is elevated above heart level — is a classic sign of aortic regurgitation.
Section 3.1

Q9. A patient has an exaggerated fall in pulse volume during inspiration, measured at 14 mmHg on sphygmomanometry. Which two conditions are most classically associated with this finding?

Pulsus paradoxus — an exaggerated fall in pulse volume on inspiration greater than 10 mmHg — is classically associated with cardiac tamponade and acute asthma.
Section 3.1

Q10. On comparing the left and right radial pulses, a physician notes a palpable delay between the two sides. Which conditions should this radio-radial delay raise concern for?

A radio-radial delay (and similarly a radio-femoral delay) is a sign of aortic coarctation or aortic dissection.

Hand Stigmata & Peripheral Pulses

While holding the patient's hand for pulse assessment, inspect it in an intentional but unobtrusive way. Well-perfused hands are symmetrically warm and similarly colored.

Peripheral Signs and Cardiac Associations
Peripheral SignDescriptionCardiac Association
ClubbingBroadening/thickening of fingertips (and toes), increased nail curvature, decreased angle between cuticle and nailInfective endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease
Splinter hemorrhagesStreak hemorrhages in the nailbeds (from micro-hemorrhage — trauma, infection, psoriatic nail disease, vasculitis)Infective endocarditis
Janeway lesionsPainless macules, only on the palms, caused by septic emboliInfective endocarditis
Osler's nodesPainful, tender nodules on the fingertipsInfective endocarditis
Pearl: extremely long fingers can be a sign of Marfan syndrome — itself a risk factor for aortic dissection.

Peripheral Pulses

Document all peripheral pulses — peripheral vascular disease is an important predictor of coronary artery disease.

  • Femoral: midinguinal point (midway between the pubic symphysis and ASIS, just inferior to the inguinal ligament)
  • Popliteal: deep in the center of the popliteal fossa, patient supine with knees bent
  • Posterior tibial: behind the medial malleolus
  • Dorsalis pedis: over the second metatarsal bone, just lateral to the extensor hallucis tendon
Section 3.2

Q11. A patient with fever has painless macular lesions on the palms and tender nodules on the fingertips. Which two findings are described, respectively, and what do they suggest?

Painless palmar macules are Janeway lesions; painful fingertip nodules are Osler's nodes. Both are stigmata of infective endocarditis.
Section 3.2

Q12. A physician wants to palpate the popliteal pulse. What is the correct technique?

The popliteal pulse is best felt deep in the center of the popliteal fossa, with the patient lying supine and their knees bent to relax the surrounding musculature.

4. Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP)

JVP Anatomy & Technique

Estimating the JVP is one of the most important and frequently used physical exam skills. The JVP closely parallels pressure in the right atrium (central venous pressure), reflecting venous system volume.

The JVP is best assessed from pulsations in the right internal jugular vein, which lies in direct line with the SVC and right atrium. The IJ veins lie deep to the sternocleidomastoid and are not directly visible — you're identifying pulsations transmitted to the neck's surface, not the vein itself.

JVP vs. carotid pulse: the dominant movement of the JVP is inward (coinciding with descent); the dominant movement of the carotid pulse is outward. Don't confuse the two.

Careful observation of JVP fluctuations gives clues about volume status, right and left ventricular function, tricuspid/pulmonary valve patency, pressure in the myocardium/pericardium, and arrhythmias from junctional rhythms or AV blocks.

Technique

  • Starting position: table/bed at 30°
  • Turn the patient's head slightly left, then right, identifying the external jugular vein on each side
  • Focus on the internal jugular venous pulsations on the right
  • Find the highest point of oscillation (the meniscus) — or the point above which the external jugular vein appears collapsed
  • JVP is measured as the vertical distance above the sternal angle (angle of Louis, around T4, where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum)

In a euvolemic patient, JVP is typically measured at about 3 cm above the sternal angle.

Section 4.1

Q13. A student is having trouble distinguishing the jugular venous pulse from the adjacent carotid pulse in the neck. Which feature reliably distinguishes the two?

The dominant movement of the JVP is inward (coinciding with descent), in contrast to the carotid pulse, whose dominant movement is outward — a key bedside distinguishing feature.
Section 4.1

Q14. Estimating the JVP is described as closely paralleling which physiologic parameter?

The JVP closely parallels the pressure in the right atrium (central venous pressure), which relates primarily to venous system volume.

Abnormal JVP

A JVP measured at more than 3 cm above the sternal angle (or more than 8 cm total distance above the right atrium) is considered elevated/abnormal.

Causes of Elevated JVP
Heart failure
Tricuspid stenosis
Chronic pulmonary hypertension
SVC obstruction
Cardiac tamponade
Constrictive pericarditis
Section 4.2

Q15. A patient's JVP is measured at 6 cm above the sternal angle. How should this finding be classified, and which conditions might explain it?

A JVP greater than 3 cm above the sternal angle (or greater than 8 cm total distance above the right atrium) is considered elevated, and can reflect heart failure, tricuspid stenosis, chronic pulmonary hypertension, SVC obstruction, cardiac tamponade, or constrictive pericarditis.
Section 4.2

Q16. A patient presents with muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and a markedly elevated JVP after a recent pericardial effusion was diagnosed. Which condition on the differential for elevated JVP is most consistent with this presentation?

Muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated JVP in the setting of a known pericardial effusion is the classic Beck's triad presentation of cardiac tamponade — one of the recognized causes of elevated JVP.

ConceptKey Point
What JVP reflectsClosely parallels right atrial pressure / central venous pressure

5. Carotid Pulse & The Back

Carotid Pulse

Always auscultate before you palpate. Carotid atherosclerosis can narrow the arteries, so listen for a bruit before palpating the pulse.

  1. Auscultate each carotid artery, asking the patient to briefly stop breathing (~10 seconds, then remember to tell them to resume) — use the diaphragm, which detects the higher-frequency bruit sound better than the bell.
    A bruit is a low-frequency swooshing sound from turbulent blood flow. In a younger patient it may be an innocent finding; in an older adult, it usually suggests carotid artery stenosis.
  2. Palpate the carotid pulse (only after confirming no bruit): press just inside the medial border of a relaxed sternocleidomastoid, roughly at the level of the thyroid cartilage. Avoid pressing directly on the carotid sinus (adjacent to the top of the thyroid cartilage — this can cause reflex hypotension). Never palpate both carotids simultaneously — this can reduce cerebral blood flow and provoke a syncopal event.

Slowly increase pressure until you feel the maximal pulsation, then slowly decrease pressure to sense the arterial pressure and contour.

Carotid Pulse Characteristics
ParameterFindingAssociation
TimingNormal upstroke follows S1, precedes S2—
AmplitudeThready/weakCardiogenic shock
AmplitudeBoundingAortic regurgitation
ContourNormal upstroke is brisk—
ContourDelayed upstrokeAortic stenosis
Section 5.1

Q17. Before palpating a patient's carotid pulse, what is the required first step, and why?

The carotid artery should always be auscultated for a bruit before palpation, since carotid atherosclerosis can narrow the artery — palpating first risks missing important information or dislodging unstable plaque.
Section 5.1

Q18. A physician accidentally presses firmly on both carotid arteries simultaneously while attempting to compare pulses. What is the most significant risk of this technique error?

Palpating both carotid arteries at the same time can decrease blood flow to the brain and provoke a syncopal event — carotids should always be palpated one side at a time.
Section 5.1

Q19. A patient has a delayed, slow-rising carotid upstroke on palpation. Which valvular lesion is most consistent with this finding?

A delayed carotid upstroke (contour) is associated with aortic stenosis, since the stenotic valve slows the rate of ejection into the aorta. This contrasts with the brisk, bounding pulse of aortic regurgitation.

The Back

Since the patient is likely already sitting upright (having just had the carotids and precordium partially assessed), take the opportunity to examine the back without repositioning the patient unnecessarily:

  • Inspect for posterior/lateral surgical scars
  • Palpate the sacrum for sacral edema — more common in patients who have been lying flat for long periods or who are immobile
  • Auscultate the lung bases for crackles/crepitations (fluid)
Pearl: sacral edema plus crepitations at the lung bases together suggest left-sided heart failure.
Section 5.2

Q20. On examination of the back, a patient has both sacral edema and crackles at the lung bases. What does this combination of findings most strongly suggest?

Sacral edema together with crepitations heard at the lung bases suggests left-sided heart failure, reflecting fluid backing up into the pulmonary circulation and dependent tissue.

Section 5 Summary Table

ConceptKey Point
Carotid exam orderAlways auscultate (diaphragm, breath held) for a bruit before palpating
BruitLow-frequency swoosh from turbulent flow; innocent in the young, suggests stenosis in older adults
Palpation techniqueMedial border of relaxed SCM at thyroid cartilage level; avoid the carotid sinus; never palpate both sides at once (stroke/syncope risk)
Carotid amplitudeThready/weak → cardiogenic shock; bounding → aortic regurgitation
Carotid contourBrisk = normal; delayed upstroke → aortic stenosis
The backInspect for scars, palpate for sacral edema, auscultate lung bases; sacral edema + basal crepitations → left-sided heart failure

6. The Precordium

Inspection & the Apical Impulse

Inspect the precordium for scars, chest wall deformities, and visible pulsations.

Precordial Scars
ScarLocationCommon Cause
Midline sternotomyMidline of the thoraxCABG, valve replacement, congenital correction
Pacemaker scarSuperior left thorax, midclavicular linePacemaker placement
Axillary thoracotomy5th intercostal space, anterior axillary linePrevious chest drain (best assessed from the back)
Posterolateral thoracotomyLateral/posterior intercostal space, inferior to the scapular tipLobectomy or pneumonectomy (best assessed from the back)

Other Visible/Palpable Abnormalities

  • Chest: deformities, heaves, visible pulsations
  • Abdomen: epigastric pulsations (RV hypertrophy, AAA); pulsatile liver (tricuspid insufficiency); splenomegaly (endocarditis)
  • Extremities: peripheral edema (CHF)

The Apical Impulse

The apical impulse represents the brief early pulsation of the left ventricle as it moves anteriorly during systole and contacts the chest wall — in most exams, this is also the point of maximal impulse (PMI).

  • Displaced (upward): pregnancy/gravid uterus, high left diaphragm
  • Laterally displaced: heart failure, cardiomyopathy, ischemic heart disease
  • Hypokinetic + left lateral displacement: dilated heart failure
  • Undetectable apical impulse: consider a large pericardial effusion
Pearl: if you can't find the apical impulse, ask the patient to exhale fully and hold their breath briefly, then reassess (remember to let them breathe again afterward). In a female patient, it may help to displace the left breast upward or laterally.
Section 6.1

Q21. A pregnant patient in her third trimester is noted to have her apical impulse shifted upward and slightly to the left compared to prior exams. What is the most likely explanation?

In pregnancy, the gravid uterus tends to shift the diaphragm upward, which can shift the apical impulse upward and to the left — a benign, expected finding rather than a pathologic displacement.
Section 6.1

Q22. A patient with known dilated cardiomyopathy has an apical impulse that is hypokinetic and displaced toward the left lateral chest wall. What does this most likely reflect?

A hypokinetic apical impulse displaced to the left lateral chest wall reflects dilated heart failure — the enlarged, weakened left ventricle shifts and weakens the impulse.
Section 6.1

Q23. A patient with a large pericardial effusion undergoes a cardiac exam. What would you expect to find regarding the apical impulse?

A large pericardial effusion may make the apical impulse undetectable, as the surrounding fluid dampens transmission of the ventricular impulse to the chest wall.

Palpation: PMI, Valve Areas & Thrills

Valve Area Landmarks
AreaLocation
Mitral area5th intercostal space, midclavicular line
Tricuspid areaLeft 5th costosternal border
Pulmonary areaLeft upper sternal border, 2nd intercostal space
Aortic areaRight upper sternal border, 2nd intercostal space

Palpate for the PMI — usually found in the left 4th or 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line — and palpate each of the four valve areas for thrills (palpable murmurs, which feel like soft vibrations) and heaves.

Section 6.2

Q24. A physician palpates a soft, buzzing vibration over the aortic area. What is this palpable finding called, and what does it usually correspond to?

A soft, vibratory sensation felt on palpation is a thrill — the palpable correlate of a (usually loud, grade 4 or higher) murmur.
Section 6.2

Q25. Where should a physician palpate to assess the tricuspid area?

The tricuspid area is located at the left 5th costosternal border, distinct from the mitral area (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line).

7. Heart Sounds

Normal & Split S2

Auscultate the four valve areas with the diaphragm (detects high-frequency sounds better than the bell), ideally while simultaneously palpating the carotid pulse — this lets you time any murmurs you hear.

S2 is composed of the aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valve closure components.

  • Physiological splitting: A2 occurs before P2, widening on inspiration — very common, especially in young patients. Mechanism: negative intrathoracic pressure on inspiration increases venous return, delaying RV emptying/P2, while pulmonary capillary pooling accelerates LV emptying/A2.
  • Reverse (paradoxical) splitting: occurs when aortic valve closure is delayed — seen in left bundle branch block or a paced right ventricle. Can also occur when pulmonary valve closure is early, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
  • Wide, fixed splitting: due to an atrial septal defect.
Section 7.1

Q26. A healthy 19-year-old has a split second heart sound that widens with inspiration and normalizes with expiration. How should this finding be interpreted?

Physiological splitting of S2 — widening on inspiration due to delayed pulmonary valve closure and accelerated aortic valve closure — is a very common, normal finding, especially in young patients.
Section 7.1

Q27. A patient with a known left bundle branch block is found to have reverse (paradoxical) splitting of S2. What is the underlying mechanism?

Reverse (paradoxical) splitting of S2 occurs when aortic valve closure is delayed, as seen in left bundle branch block or a paced right ventricle — causing P2 to occur before the (now-delayed) A2.
Section 7.1

Q28. A wide, fixed split of S2 that does not vary with respiration is classically associated with which congenital condition?

A wide, fixed splitting of S2 (unchanged with respiration) is due to an atrial septal defect.

S3, S4, Clicks & Opening Snap

  • S3: heard soon after S2, from rapid, high-volume filling of the left ventricle. Seen in left ventricular failure, but also in very athletic hearts or high-volume states like pregnancy.
  • S4: heard just before S1, caused by atrial contraction filling a stiff left ventricle. Seen in hypertensive heart disease or diastolic heart failure.
  • Opening snap: heard after S2, due to a diseased mitral valve opening into a stenotic position — as in mitral valve stenosis.
  • Ejection click: heard soon after S1, due to aortic stenosis, aortic sclerosis, or pulmonary stenosis.
Section 7.2

Q29. A 68-year-old with long-standing hypertension is found to have an extra heart sound just before S1. Which additional heart sound is this, and what is its mechanism?

S4 occurs just before S1, caused by atrial contraction filling a stiff, non-compliant left ventricle — classically seen in hypertensive heart disease or diastolic heart failure.
Section 7.2

Q30. A young, competitive athlete is found to have an S3 on routine cardiac exam, with no other symptoms or abnormal findings. How should this be interpreted?

While S3 can indicate left ventricular failure from rapid, high-volume ventricular filling, it can also be heard in normal, high-volume physiologic states — including the very athletic heart and pregnancy — so clinical context matters.
Section 7.2

Q31. A patient has a diseased mitral valve that opens into a stenotic position. Which added heart sound would this classically produce, and when is it heard?

An opening snap is heard after S2, caused by a diseased mitral valve opening into a stenotic position — the classic added sound of mitral valve stenosis.

Section 7 Summary Table

SoundTimingMechanism / Association
Physiological S2 splitA2 before P2, widens on inspirationNormal, common in young patients; ↑ venous return delays P2, pooling accelerates A2
Reverse (paradoxical) splitP2 before A2Delayed aortic closure (LBBB, paced RV) or early pulmonary closure (WPW)
Wide, fixed splitUnchanged with respirationAtrial septal defect
S3Soon after S2Rapid high-volume LV filling — LV failure, athletic heart, pregnancy

8. Murmurs & Putting It All Together

Murmur Timing, Shape & Grading

Determine if a murmur is systolic or diastolic by timing it against the carotid pulse. Then determine its length (early/mid/late) and shape.

Generally, systolic murmurs tend to be either midsystolic or pansystolic.

Pearl: midsystolic murmurs can be functional (innocent) — short, and decreasing in intensity with maneuvers that reduce LV volume (standing, sitting up, Valsalva straining). These are often heard in healthy patients and are not pathologic.
Grading Systolic Murmurs (6-Point Scale)
GradeDescription
1/6Softer in volume than S1 and S2, very faint
2/6Equal in volume to S1 and S2, quiet, but heard immediately
3/6Louder in volume than S1 and S2, moderately loud
4/6Louder in volume than S1 and S2, with a palpable thrill
5/6Louder still, with thrill; may be heard with the stethoscope partly off the chest
6/6Louder still, with thrill; may be heard with the stethoscope entirely off the chest
Grading Diastolic Murmurs (4-Point Scale)
GradeDescription
1/4Barely audible
2/4Faint but immediately audible
3/4Easily heard
4/4Very loud
Pearl: diastolic murmurs are graded on a 4-point (not 6-point) scale, because diastolic murmurs usually do not associate with a palpable thrill.

A machine-like or continuous murmur suggests a few underlying diagnoses: an AV fistula (e.g., in a dialysis patient), or a congenital patent ductus arteriosus in a young patient. Venous hums and pericardial friction rubs also have both systolic and diastolic components.

Supplemental video resources: the course's supplemental videos demonstrate live auscultation technique (e.g., tricuspid stenosis at the left lower sternal border with the bell), an overview of heart sounds and murmurs, and a walkthrough of the major murmurs (aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, and Erb's point) — well worth watching alongside this guide before the CV skills block.
Section 8.1

Q32. A murmur is heard that begins with S1 and stops precisely at S2, with no audible gap between the murmur and either heart sound. How should this murmur be classified?

A pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur starts with S1 and stops at S2, without a gap between the murmur and the heart sounds — distinguishing it from a midsystolic murmur, which has audible gaps before S2.
Section 8.1

Q33. A murmur is auscultated with a palpable thrill, and it can still be heard faintly even when the stethoscope is lifted slightly off the chest wall. What grade should this systolic murmur be assigned?

A systolic murmur with a thrill that can still be heard when the stethoscope is partly off the chest is Grade 5/6 — Grade 6/6 requires audibility with the stethoscope entirely off the chest.
Section 8.1

Q34. A young patient is found to have a continuous, machine-like murmur heard throughout systole and diastole. Which congenital condition classically produces this finding?

A machine-like, continuous murmur in a young patient is classically caused by a congenital patent ductus arteriosus, since blood continues to flow across the ductus throughout both systole and diastole.
Section 8.1

Q35. A short midsystolic murmur is noted in an asymptomatic teenager. The murmur decreases in intensity when the patient stands up. How should this most likely be characterized?

Short midsystolic murmurs that decrease in intensity with maneuvers reducing left ventricular volume (standing, sitting, Valsalva) are classically functional (innocent) murmurs, commonly heard in healthy patients and not pathologic.

Putting It All Together

Throughout the cardiovascular exam, keep asking yourself the following questions to systematically assess the integrity of the patient's heart pump:

  • Is forward pump function normal? Is the blood pressure in the normal range?
  • Are the extremities well perfused? Are the pulses brisk and easily palpable?
  • Is the JVP normal? Is there edema in the lower extremities?
  • Is the heart normal in size? Is the PMI displaced or over the right ventricle?
  • Is there evidence of valvular heart disease? Are there systolic and/or diastolic murmurs?
  • Can you distinguish findings of pulmonary edema?

A detailed, careful clinical examination can reveal much about the condition of a patient's heart, and documenting findings well will greatly facilitate any referrals or further investigations needed. In an era of abundant technology, skilled bedside examination still offers the best combination of convenience, safety, and cost-effective care. A good history and physical exam will never fail you or your patient.

Further Investigations

  • ECG: electrical activity, arrhythmias, infarction
  • Echocardiogram: structure/function of the heart, valve disease
Section 8.2

Q36. After completing a thorough cardiovascular exam, a physician wants to further evaluate for arrhythmias and evidence of prior infarction. Which further investigation is most appropriate?

An ECG assesses electrical activity, arrhythmias, and evidence of infarction — the appropriate next step for these specific concerns, distinct from an echocardiogram, which primarily assesses structure/function and valve disease.
Section 8.2

Q37. Which of the following best reflects the overall philosophy emphasized throughout this lecture regarding the physical exam versus available technology?

Despite advancing technology, a good history and physical exam remains valuable — supporting timely diagnosis, safety, and cost-effective care, with clinical signs guiding which further investigations (like ECG or echocardiogram) are actually needed.

Master Summary Table — The Full Cardiovascular Exam

Exam ComponentKey TechniquesKey Abnormal Findings
Setup & Vitals Consent, 45° bed, BP in both arms + sitting/standing Arm BP difference → aortic dissection; postural drop → orthostatic hypotension
General Inspection Work of breathing, color, bedside clues, facial signs Cyanosis (R→L shunt), pallor (anemia), malar flush (mitral stenosis), proptosis (afib), scars (CABG/pacemaker)
Hands & Pulses Radial pulse rate/rhythm, radio-radial delay, collapsing pulse test, peripheral pulses Irregular → afib; collapsing pulse → AR; clubbing/Janeway/Osler → endocarditis
JVP Right IJ, 30°, measure height above sternal angle >3 cm above sternal angle → heart failure, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstruction
Carotid & Back Auscultate (bruit) before palpating; one side at a time; check the back Bruit (stenosis); delayed upstroke (AS); bounding (AR); sacral edema + basal crackles → L heart failure
Precordium Inspect scars/pulsations → palpate PMI & 4 valve areas → auscultate Displaced/hypokinetic PMI → failure/cardiomyopathy; thrill → loud murmur
Heart Sounds Time against carotid pulse; listen for splitting and extra sounds Fixed split → ASD; S3 → volume overload/failure; S4 → stiff LV; opening snap → MS
Murmurs Time, shape, grade (6-pt systolic / 4-pt diastolic) Pansystolic vs. midsystolic; continuous → PDA/AV fistula; thrill → grade ≥4/6
